extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examiner evaluation of patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 using MPEP Chapter 2100: determine whether claims fall into statutory categories and whether they are directed to judicial exceptions under the Alice/Mayo two-part framework (Steps 1, 2A, and 2B). Focuses on claim construction (BRI), identifying exceptions, Prong One/Two analysis, and handling multiple exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 1: Whether a claim is to a statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1 asks whether the claim is to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter (the four statutory categories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should be made after determining what the inventor has invented by reviewing the entire application disclosure and construing the claims in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI). If the claim as a whole does not fall within any statutory category (Step 1: NO) it is non-statutory and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. If the claim as a whole falls within one or more statutory categories (Step 1: YES) it proceeds to further analysis at Step 2A. Examples: transitory propagating signals (Nuijten) and certain machine-readable media that encompass carrier waves (Mentor Graphics) may be non-statutory. When a claim fails Step 1 but an amendment could place it within a statutory category, recommend amendment; use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 and see MPEP §2106.07(a)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of claim construction and review of entire disclosure (BRI) before eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Before performing eligibility (Step 1 or Step 2A) examiners must determine what the inventor has invented by reviewing the entire disclosure and construing claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2106 subsection II and MPEP §2111 for BRI. Eligibility evaluation is dependent on properly understanding claim scope; examiners should point out BRI issues and suggest narrowing amendments where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims whose BRI covers both statutory and non‑statutory embodiments fail Step 1
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim whose BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non-statutory subject matter (Step 1: NO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When BRI encompasses non-statutory embodiments (e.g., machine-readable medium that covers carrier waves and physical media), a §101 rejection is appropriate. Best practice: point out the BRI on the record and recommend an amendment to narrow the claim to statutory embodiments if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: When claim is clearly not within the four categories — rejection practice
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is clearly not within one of the four statutory categories (Step 1: NO), then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 must be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01; see MPEP §2106.07(a)(1). If the disclosure indicates the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, continue analysis to determine whether such amended claim would be eligible and recommend amendment if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 2A: Whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A asks whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception — a law of nature, a natural phenomenon (product of nature), or an abstract idea. If the claim as a whole is not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO), it is eligible at Pathway B; if it is directed to an exception (Step 2A: YES), further analysis at Step 2B is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the first part of the Alice/Mayo two-part framework. Evaluation should be made after claim construction (BRI) and review of the disclosure. See MPEP §2106 subsections III and II for procedural flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions and the underlying concern of preemption
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicially recognized exceptions include abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena (also described as physical phenomena, products of nature, scientific principles, mental processes, etc.). The Supreme Court's rationale for excluding these is the concern over preemption of basic tools of scientific and technological work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preemption is the concern underlying the exceptions but is not a standalone test for eligibility. Use the Alice/Mayo test (Steps 2A and 2B) to resolve preemption issues. Even newly discovered phenomena or novel algorithms can be exceptions; novelty alone does not satisfy §101. See cited cases (Alice, Mayo, Myriad, Flook, Benson, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A is a two‑prong inquiry (Prong One and Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A consists of Prong One: whether the claim recites a judicial exception; and Prong Two: whether the recited exception is integrated into a practical application by additional elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform Prong One first; if an exception is recited, perform Prong Two to determine if the claim as a whole integrates that exception into a practical application. If the claim does not recite an exception, the claim is not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — identifying whether a claim recites an exception (set forth or described)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong One asks whether the claim 'recites' (i.e., 'sets forth' or 'describes') an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon — meaning an identifiable judicial exception is stated or described in the claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are two ways an exception can be recited: 'set forth' (explicitly stated, e.g., a mathematical equation in Diehr) or 'described' (the concept is described but not named, e.g., intermediated settlement in Alice). Examiners should identify the specific claim limitation(s) believed to recite an exception and determine whether those limitations fall within judicial exceptions. Distinguish claims that 'recite' an exception from claims that merely 'involve' an exception (the latter do not require further eligibility analysis). Examples: a claim reciting 'F=ma' sets forth a law of nature (Prong One YES); a teeter-totter claim merely involves the law of the lever (Prong One NO). See MPEP §2106.04(a)/(b)/(c) for detailed guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — practical application/integration of the exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong Two asks whether the additional elements in the claim integrate the recited judicial exception into a practical application of that exception. If they do, the claim is not directed to the exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B; if they do not, the claim is directed to the exception (Step 2A: YES) and proceeds to Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional elements must 'integrate' the exception into a practical application or otherwise transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (Alice: 'transform the nature of the claim'). Mere recitation of a judicial exception or mere addition of another judicial exception is insufficient. See RecogniCorp, Genetic Technologies and related case law. If no additional elements exist, the claim cannot be eligible and examiner should consider recommending amendment. For details on evaluating 'integration into a practical application' see MPEP §2106.04(d)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere recitation vs. integration: additional elements cannot be another judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Where additional claim elements merely recite another judicial exception or are otherwise only the judicial exception itself, that is insufficient to integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: adding one abstract idea (math) to another abstract idea (encoding/decoding) does not render the claim non-abstract (RecogniCorp). The additional elements must do more — change the claim's nature or provide a practical application — either at Prong Two or in Step 2B (inventive concept).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating claims reciting multiple judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may recite multiple judicial exceptions (e.g., two abstract ideas or two laws of nature). Examiners should apply the same eligibility analysis regardless of the number of exceptions recited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless it is clear that the claim recites distinct exceptions (e.g., a law of nature and an abstract idea), care should be taken not to parse the claim into multiple exceptions. If distinct exceptions are present, examiners may select one exception to analyze for efficiency; if analysis shows the claim integrates or amounts to significantly more than the selected exception, the claim is eligible. If multiple abstract ideas/laws are present but not distinct, consider the limitations together as a single abstract idea for Prong Two and Step 2B. See examples and case law (Bilski, Mayo, Ambry Genetics, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated groupings of abstract ideas for examiner use
rubrics_metrics.description: To facilitate examination, the Office has enumerated groupings of abstract ideas: (1) mathematical concepts; (2) certain methods of organizing human activity; and (3) mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These groupings distill case law and shift examiners away from a strict case-comparison approach. Examiners should (1) identify the specific claim limitation(s) believed to recite an abstract idea and (2) determine whether those limitations fall within at least one enumeration. If they do, the claim requires further analysis in Prong Two. If they do not, the claim does not recite an abstract idea (subject to rare circumstances in MPEP §2106.04(a)(3)). Examples and subdefinitions: mathematical relationships/formulas/calculations; fundamental economic principles, commercial/legal interactions, advertising/marketing/sales activities; mental observations/evaluations/judgments. See MPEP §2106.04(a)(2) for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software and business‑method clarifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Software and business methods are not categorically excluded from §101 and are not automatically abstract ideas merely because they involve calculations or business practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (Enfish, McRO, Thales Visionix, Content Extraction) shows that claims to software or business methods can be eligible if they do not recite or are not directed to judicial exceptions as a whole. Examiners should apply the enumerated groupings and the Prong One/Two analysis rather than blanket assumptions about software or business-method claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of complete preemption is not dispositive of eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: While preemption is the underlying concern with judicial exceptions, the mere absence of complete preemption does not demonstrate that a claim is eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Alice/Mayo test must be applied; finding some non-preemptive scope does not obviate the need for the two-part analysis. Courts have rejected arguments that limited preemption implies eligibility (Diehr discussion). Several Federal Circuit decisions have noted lack of preemption where claims were found eligible, but preemption analysis should be resolved through the two-part test (steps 2A/2B).

rubrics_metrics.name: If claim recites an exception and no additional elements exist, claim cannot be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites only a judicial exception without additional elements that integrate it into a practical application cannot be eligible under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases make the appropriate rejection (see MPEP §2106.07) and a best practice is to recommend an amendment, if possible, that would resolve eligibility by adding qualifying elements.
